reasons: Only 1894 of 3277 lines and 40 of 69 sections are visible in this packet, so the rest is unreviewed.
No tests or error handling are visible in the reviewed part.
The palm drawing step temporarily swaps the drawing target and does not restore it if an error occurs.
Much of the painting runs at load time and may be slow on weak devices.

terms.meaning: a drawing area on a web page that code paints onto pixel by pixel
a hidden drawing area used to build a picture before it is shown
a starting number that makes a random sequence repeat the same way every time
a formula that produces a repeatable list of numbers that look random
a smooth curve shaped by a few control points
limiting drawing so that it only appears inside a chosen shape
a single shared object that the whole program reuses
a browser setting that asks sites to reduce animation for people who need it
the time that passed since the previous animation frame
a thick, textured paint look created with many small strokes

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: File header and origin note
sections.what: A header comment says the engine was ported from a design HTML file and must keep its seeds, curves and behaviour exactly. It does not run anything itself.
sections.why: The code states that it was ported verbatim from the design file.
sections.watch_out: Changing random seeds or fixed numbers changes how the village looks.

sections.name: MapInstance
sections.title: Shape of one drawn map view
sections.what: Describes one on-screen map: its id, the container it sits in, its drawing canvas, its size, its pixel density, an optional mini map and the visible area.
sections.why: Lets the engine draw onto several maps at once.
sections.watch_out: The mini map canvas is optional and may be null, so callers must check it before use.

sections.name: VillageSimulationEngine
sections.title: Public controls of the village engine
sections.what: Lists the functions other code may call: register a map, set the pointer position, export the survey map as an image, draw satellite thumbnails, and check or wait for readiness.
sections.why: Gives the rest of the app one clear entry point into the animation.
sections.watch_out: The engine is shared. Calling its functions before it reports ready may give incomplete output.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 1)
sections.title: Engine start and seeded randomness
sections.what: Returns the existing engine if one was already built. Otherwise it sets up the repeatable random number generator, the main size values, and reads whether the user asked for reduced motion.
sections.why: A fixed seed makes the village look the same on every load. Likely reason for the reduced-motion check: accessibility. How that flag is used is not visible in this section.
sections.watch_out: Every random call uses the same sequence, so adding or moving one random call shifts every element that comes after it.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Shape helpers for paths and points
sections.what: Helpers to test whether a point is inside a shape, smooth a list of points into a curve, turn points into a drawable path, and measure the distance from a point to a shape outline.
sections.why: Water, roads and fields are described as lists of points, so these tools are needed everywhere.
sections.watch_out: The smoothing helper behaves differently for closed shapes and open lines, so the correct flag must be passed.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Distance, centre and painting canvas setup
sections.what: Adds helpers for finding a centre point and blending two points, creates the hidden painting canvas at a larger size, and defines the basic brush stroke that all painted marks use.
sections.why: Likely reason: painting happens on a hidden canvas first and is then copied to the visible maps.
sections.watch_out: The painting canvas is only created when a document exists, so painting helpers must check it before drawing.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 4)
sections.title: Historic site and main lake outline
sections.what: Adds streak detail to brush strokes, a fixed six-point historic area that placement avoids, and the outline of the main lake.
sections.why: The historic area appears to be a protected spot that other items must avoid. The code does not say so directly.
sections.watch_out: The lake outline is a hand-set list of points, so reshaping the lake means editing those numbers carefully.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Pond and island outlines
sections.what: Builds the outlines of the two islands and a second pond from fixed points with a small random wobble.
sections.why: Gives the water and land a natural, uneven shape.
sections.watch_out: Random wobble is applied to the pond shape, so its exact outline depends on the random sequence.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Combined water shape and land check
sections.what: Joins all the water outlines into one shape and checks whether a point is in water, with the islands treated as land.
sections.why: Many placement and drawing steps ask whether a spot is water.
sections.watch_out: This exact check is slow. A faster lookup is built later, so the two must agree.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 7)
sections.title: Water lookup map and roads
sections.what: Builds a black and white picture of where water is, so water checks are fast. It also defines the two dirt roads as lists of points.
sections.why: Likely reason: checking shapes for every point would be slow, so a precomputed picture is used.
sections.watch_out: The water picture is only made when a document exists. Without it, the slower exact check runs instead.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 8)
sections.title: Road nearness and field layout
sections.what: Checks whether a spot is close to a road, then builds a grid of slightly irregular field plots. Some plots are split in two, and the crop type is picked by weighted chance.
sections.why: Creates the patchwork farmland look.
sections.watch_out: The crop weights are set to add up to one. Changing one weight changes the odds for every crop.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Choosing a crop and drawing crop rows
sections.what: Picks a crop type by weighted chance and draws evenly spaced lines across a field.
sections.why: The rows suggest planting and make each field look worked.
sections.watch_out: The order of the crop list affects the random pick, so reordering it changes which crop appears where.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 10)
sections.title: Preparing one field shape
sections.what: Prepares a field outline with slightly rough edges, picks its colour, and limits drawing to that shape so brush marks stay inside.
sections.why: Rough edges make the field look hand-painted.
sections.watch_out: The minimum and maximum calls pass 0 as the this value. This works, but it is unusual and easy to break when edited.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 11)
sections.title: Base strokes and crop marks
sections.what: Adds base colour strokes to a field, then extra marks for rice paddies, young crops, fallow land, vegetables and mustard.
sections.why: Each crop type looks different on the map.
sections.watch_out: Crop types not listed here get only the base strokes, which is probably intended but is not stated.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: if
sections.title: Wheat, cane and field edge marks
sections.what: Adds wheat and sugarcane marks, restores the drawing state after the field is done, and adds small dark marks along the field edges.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond giving those crops their own look and edges their own marks.
sections.watch_out: Drawing state must be restored after clipping, or later marks will be cut off by the field shape.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 13)
sections.title: Village layout containers and hut spacing
sections.what: Defines what a hut is and creates lists for huts, trees, palms, cows and hay stacks. A helper checks whether a spot is clear of existing huts.
sections.why: Keeps placed items from overlapping.
sections.watch_out: Hut spacing depends on hut width, so changing hut size changes how close huts can sit.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Placing huts and first trees
sections.what: Scatters huts across set zones while avoiding water, the historic area, the pond, roads and each other. Some huts get a hay stack. It also adds four fixed trees and a helper that decides whether a tree spot is acceptable.
sections.why: The placement rules keep the village looking realistic.
sections.watch_out: Each zone gets a fixed number of tries, so crowded zones may end up with fewer huts than the target.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Scattering trees and palms
sections.what: Adds more trees across the zones and a set of random trees, sorts all trees by their vertical position so lower trees draw in front, and places palms near the shore or roads.
sections.why: Sorting by height on the page makes trees overlap in a believable way.
sections.watch_out: Sorting changes draw order, so trees added later in the list may appear behind earlier ones.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Placing cows and painting roads
sections.what: Places up to 12 cows in a zone away from water and huts, then paints the two roads as dusty brown strokes in chunks of 50 points.
sections.why: The cows add life to the scene. Likely reason for chunked painting: keeps each queued step small.
sections.watch_out: Chunk size controls how many painting steps are queued for the roads, so changing it changes load work.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 17)
sections.title: Water colour layers
sections.what: Adds rough coloured patches inside water shapes, and a base layer with a dark outline and a soft radial gradient.
sections.why: Gives the water a painted depth instead of a flat fill.
sections.watch_out: Each water chunk adds many marks, so the number of chunks has a direct effect on load time.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 18)
sections.title: Shoreline edges and the start of hut drawing
sections.what: Paints a dark band and small marks around the water edge, then begins drawing huts by placing a soft shadow under each one.
sections.why: The shore band makes the water edge read clearly. Reason for the shadow not stated in the code beyond adding depth.
sections.watch_out: Shore marks are placed by random tries, so the number of marks depends on the seed.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: if
sections.title: Hut walls and roofs
sections.what: Draws a courtyard patch when the hut has one, then the two-tone roof, then roof details: tile lines, thatch strokes or flat outlines.
sections.why: Three roof types give the village variety.
sections.watch_out: Roof type is picked at random when huts are placed, so changing the thresholds changes the mix of roofs.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: if
sections.title: Hut outline and tree canopy
sections.what: Adds a ridge line and a thin outline to each hut, then starts drawing a tree with a dark shadow and a rounded canopy.
sections.why: The outline helps huts stand apart from the fields.
sections.watch_out: Larger trees get extra streak detail through the last argument, so check what that flag does before changing it.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Tree shading and palm shadows
sections.what: Adds lighter and darker leaf clusters to each tree, and defines the soft shadow drawn under palm trees.
sections.why: Leaf clusters give trees depth and a sense of light from one side.
sections.watch_out: Leaf clusters use random positions, so the look of each tree depends on the seed.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Palm fronds and start of the paint queue
sections.what: Draws palm fronds as curved strokes with a small trunk dot, then starts the ordered list of painting steps: base colour, grass marks, and field patches sorted by position.
sections.why: The list is how the engine controls which item appears on top of which.
sections.watch_out: Steps run in list order, so moving one step changes what sits above it in the final picture.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Haze, roads and lake painting steps
sections.what: Queues soft haze over the scene, queues the road painting in pieces, and queues the lake base, its 26 colour chunks and its shore.
sections.why: Haze softens the scene and the lake is the largest water feature.
sections.watch_out: The lake alone queues 26 chunks of 140 marks each, which is a large amount of drawing at load time.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 24)
sections.title: Islands and upper water painting steps
sections.what: Queues the two islands, which get an earthy fill and dark outline, then queues the first pond and the upper water in the same base, chunk and shore pattern.
sections.why: Islands are queued after the lake so they sit on top of it.
sections.watch_out: If the island order moves before the lake, the lake paint will cover the islands.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 25)
sections.title: Second pond, steps and small shrine
sections.what: Queues the second pond in the same pattern, then draws four small steps and a small shrine with a green dot and a tiny flag at a fixed spot by the water.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The shrine and steps are placed at fixed coordinates.
sections.watch_out: The steps and shrine use fixed positions, so if the water outline moves, they may end up floating away from the edge.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Queueing huts, stacks, cows and trees
sections.what: Queues huts in groups of three, then the hay stacks and cows, then trees in groups of three. It also sets up an empty list for palm pictures.
sections.why: Trees are queued after huts so their canopies draw over the huts.
sections.watch_out: Queue order sets what sits on top. Moving the tree steps before the hut steps would hide the trees behind the huts.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Preparing palm pictures and the texture pass
sections.what: For each palm, draws its shadow, then draws the palm onto a small separate picture that can be reused. It then starts the thick-paint texture pass by saving a copy of the current picture.
sections.why: Separate palm pictures let the palms be reused and animated later.
sections.watch_out: The drawing target is swapped while each palm is drawn and is only restored at the end. An error in between leaves later drawing on the wrong canvas.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Thick paint texture and light wash
sections.what: Adds many small thick-paint strokes over the picture, using colours sampled from the saved copy with small shifts. It then lays a warm light gradient over the whole scene.
sections.why: Gives the scene a painted, textured surface.
sections.watch_out: Each texture pass reads a full copy of the picture, so the two passes are costly on load.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 29)
sections.title: Grain texture and moving-scene setup
sections.what: Adds a faint grain over the whole picture, then prepares shimmer points on the water, a list of ripples, smoke sources from a few huts, and three drifting cloud shapes.
sections.why: Grain and clouds make the scene feel less flat. Reason for the smoke selection not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The smoke source selection uses an unusual chain of filters that is not explained, so change it carefully.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 30)
sections.title: Flock routes and pointer state
sections.what: Stores the current pointer position and defines three bird flocks, each with a route, a size, a duration and a repeat period.
sections.why: Flocks cross the scene on a repeating schedule.
sections.watch_out: The code assumes each repeat period is at least as long as the flight duration, and does not check this.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Creating flying and resting birds
sections.what: Creates each flock member at an offset so the group spreads out in a line, then places up to 11 resting birds near the water edge, keeping them apart from each other.
sections.why: The offsets give the flock a natural spread and the resting birds add quiet life.
sections.watch_out: Resting spots are chosen by random tries with a fixed limit, so fewer birds appear if few suitable spots exist.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 32)
sections.title: Moving flock birds and scaring them
sections.what: Each frame, moves flock birds along their route with a small wobble. When the pointer comes close, they are pushed away. The resting birds also begin the scare check.
sections.why: Responding to the pointer is the main interactive feature of the scene.
sections.watch_out: Movement depends on the time step, so a very large time step can make birds jump.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 33)
sections.title: Birds fleeing and returning home
sections.what: A scared resting bird lifts off, turns and flies away, then flies back to its home spot and settles. The wing-beat phase is also advanced each frame so the wings flap.
sections.why: Shows the birds reacting to the pointer and then calming down.
sections.watch_out: A returning bird checks the pointer again, so it can flip between fleeing and returning while the pointer stays near.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 34)
sections.title: Drawing one wing and the bird pose
sections.what: Draws a single wing from a curved shape, and starts drawing a bird by setting its size, angle and wing position from the flap phase.
sections.why: The wing shape is redrawn each frame to show movement.
sections.watch_out: The same drawing function is used for the bird shadow and the bird itself, so the shadow flag must be respected when editing.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: if
sections.title: Drawing the bird body and beak
sections.what: Draws the wings, body, head and beak of a flying bird. In shadow mode it uses a single flat colour and skips the detail.
sections.why: Gives each bird a recognisable shape.
sections.watch_out: Any change to the body must be checked in both normal and shadow modes.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 36)
sections.title: Drawing a resting bird
sections.what: Draws a sitting bird with a soft shadow and a head that dips up and down in a repeating motion, as if pecking.
sections.why: The pecking motion makes resting birds look alive.
sections.watch_out: The pecking uses a shared time value offset by each bird, so birds are out of step only by their own offset.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 37)
sections.title: Drawing all birds and the wind sprite
sections.what: Draws bird shadows first, then resting birds, then flying birds on top. It also prepares a soft light picture and 46 drifting leaves in random autumn colours, then starts the wind drawing.
sections.why: Drawing the shadows underneath makes the birds look like they are above the ground.
sections.watch_out: Draw order is important: moving the shadow pass above the birds would put shadows on top of them.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: if
sections.title: Wind streaks, falling leaves and palm sway
sections.what: Draws faint moving wind streaks across the village picture, then drifting leaves that float across and loop back to the edge. It also makes the palm trees sway slightly. A user sees these as the background coming alive.
sections.why: Likely reason: adds gentle motion to the static painted village so it feels alive. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Leaves wrap around using fixed edges built from the map size constants, so changing the map size means these edges must be checked too.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 39)
sections.title: Boats and their water ripples
sections.what: Defines three boats with fixed start points, speeds and colours, works out where each boat is at a given moment, and draws the faint rings it leaves on the water. A user sees boats gliding back and forth on the lake.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives the water scene movement without needing animation frames stored in advance. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Boat paths are fixed numbers, not checked against the shape of the water, so a boat could drift onto land if the numbers change.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 40)
sections.title: Boat drawing and road length setup
sections.what: Draws a boat hull with a small sari-coloured figure and an oar that moves. It also measures the total length of each road so walkers can move along it by distance.
sections.why: The road lengths are needed so people and dogs can move smoothly along a path. The boat hull is drawn to match the wake from the previous section.
sections.watch_out: The road length helper assumes each road is a list of points in order; a badly ordered road would make walkers jump.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 41)
sections.title: Road position lookup and walker colours
sections.what: Given a distance along a road, finds the exact point and direction on it. It also defines the palette of clothing colours and the shape of a walker, then creates an empty list for walkers.
sections.why: Likely reason: a single lookup lets every walker, dog and farmer stay on the road without storing each position. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The distance is clamped to the road's length, so a walker at the end of a road stops there rather than leaving it.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Creating villagers walking on roads
sections.what: Creates 14 walkers spread across two roads, each with random speed, direction, clothing, and optional pot, bundle or child look. It then adds four walkers that follow close behind some of the first ones. A user sees a crowd of people walking the village lanes.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed group of walkers makes the village feel busy. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Walkers are created with a seeded random source, so changing the order of random calls elsewhere changes who appears where.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Creating dogs and field candidates
sections.what: Creates four dogs on the roads with random speed, rest times and colours. It also starts a setup step that picks fields suitable for farmers and ploughs: inside a central area, not in water, not near huts or roads.
sections.why: The filter keeps farmers and ploughs off water, away from houses and away from roads so they look natural.
sections.watch_out: The field selection uses a name `g` for direction that is not defined in the visible lines, so its exact value is unclear from this packet.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Placing farmers and ploughs in fields
sections.what: Shuffles the suitable fields, then puts farmers in the first six (two people in some) and ploughs in the next two. A user sees farmers and oxen-drawn ploughs working in the fields.
sections.why: Shuffling makes different fields get farmers each time the picture is built. The number of farmers and ploughs is fixed here.
sections.watch_out: If fewer than eight suitable fields exist, some slots will be empty or filled from the wrong set. The packet does not show what happens then.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Placing grazing cattle and drawing shadows
sections.what: Tries up to 3000 random spots and places up to nine cows or buffalo on dry land near the village, each with a home area they wander around. It also defines the helper that paints soft ground shadows under things.
sections.why: Likely reason: a limited number of random tries keeps setup fast even when space is tight. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: If the land is crowded, fewer than nine cattle may appear, and the code gives no warning when this happens.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 46)
sections.title: Drawing a villager figure
sections.what: Draws one person from simple shapes: legs, a body, arms and a head. Options change the look for children, bent-over people, hats, walking poses, pots, and bundles.
sections.why: Drawing people from shapes keeps the picture light, so it runs smoothly on a web page.
sections.watch_out: The option names are checked only by the shape of the drawing, so a typo in an option name is silently ignored.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: if
sections.title: Hats, pots, bundles and cow body
sections.what: Adds the optional hat, water pot and bundle to a villager figure. Then it starts drawing a cow as an oval body that can be tinted when the cow is marked as unusual.
sections.why: These props make each villager look different without needing separate pictures.
sections.watch_out: The cow starts its drawing with a transform step that must be undone at the end. Changing one part without the other will shift everything after it.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: if
sections.title: Cow markings and head
sections.what: Finishes drawing a cow: adds the patches, the tail, and the head, which bobs up and down when the cow grazes. The head and marks change depending on whether the cow is marked as unusual.
sections.why: Different patches make each cow look distinct.
sections.watch_out: The head position depends on the grazing flag. Reason not stated in the code for the exact offsets.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 49)
sections.title: Drawing a dog
sections.what: Draws a small dog with a body, head, ears and tail. The legs bounce a little when the dog is moving.
sections.why: Likely reason: dogs add small life to the roads without needing an image file.
sections.watch_out: Dog size is fixed by one scale number, so changing that number changes every part of the dog together.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 50)
sections.title: Drawing a plough pulled by cows
sections.what: Draws a plough as a line with two cows yoked to it and a person walking behind. The plough moves back and forth across its field.
sections.why: Likely reason: shows farm work in the fields without any real movement logic outside this function.
sections.watch_out: The plough and cows are placed by direction math. A change to the plough length could make the cows leave the field edge.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 51)
sections.title: Animating farmers, ploughs and cattle
sections.what: Each frame, moves and draws the farmers swaying in place, the ploughs, and the cattle. Cattle wander slowly near home, pause, then pick a new spot nearby. Water is avoided when choosing new spots.
sections.why: Small random pauses make the cattle look like real animals grazing, not a constant march.
sections.watch_out: Cattle movement depends on the elapsed time between frames. A very long pause could make them jump, but the time step is capped by the caller.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 52)
sections.title: Animating walkers and dogs, starting the living layer
sections.what: Each frame, moves and draws the walkers, who turn around at the end of their road, and the dogs, who run, rest and sometimes turn back. It then starts the drawing of the living scene, including slow moving clouds and clipping the water area.
sections.why: Walkers and dogs reverse at road ends so they never leave the path. Clipping keeps the water effects inside the lake shape.
sections.watch_out: Walkers use a random chance to pause that depends on frame time. The frame time is capped elsewhere, so pauses stay predictable.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Water shimmer, ripples, boats and chimney smoke
sections.what: Draws sparkles on the water, expanding ripple rings from random points, the boat wakes and hulls, and small puffs of smoke. Then it updates the time step and calls the subfunctions for life, palms, wind and birds.
sections.why: These small effects make the water and village feel alive without heavy animation.
sections.watch_out: Ripple spots use plain Math.random, not the seeded random source used for the layout, so the ripples differ every run and cannot be reproduced for testing.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 54)
sections.title: Scaling the painted picture to a view
sections.what: Works out how to scale and place the painted background so it fits a view. Then, for each display, it fills the background, paints the picture and draws the living layer on top when the painting is ready.
sections.why: Each map area on the page can have a different size, so the picture is scaled to fit each one.
sections.watch_out: The draw step quits early when the display has no width or the painting is not ready, so a blank canvas usually means one of those checks failed.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: if
sections.title: Drawing the painting in timed steps
sections.what: Paints the background in small batches over about 2.6 seconds, so the page does not freeze. With reduced motion turned on, it finishes everything at once and skips the animation. When done, it marks the engine as ready and copies a small thumbnail.
sections.why: Spreading work across frames keeps the page responsive. Reduced-motion users get the finished picture immediately.
sections.watch_out: The list of paint steps named `ops` is not defined in the visible lines, so this section depends on code the packet does not show.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 56)
sections.title: Paper background, fields and roads on survey sheet
sections.what: Creates the old-paper survey map: a cream background with faint stains, then a soft green tint on each field that is not in water, then the outlines of the fields and the roads drawn as double lines.
sections.why: Likely reason: the survey look is built from a painted map so it looks like a real scanned sheet.
sections.watch_out: The survey map is drawn with random tints from a seeded source, so the colours are fixed for a given seed but would change if the seed changes.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 57)
sections.title: Water hatching and islands on survey sheet
sections.what: Fills the lake and ponds with pale blue and hand-drawn wavy lines, then outlines them. It also draws the islands in a warm beige with a blue outline.
sections.why: Hatching is the usual map style for water, so the water reads clearly on paper.
sections.watch_out: The hatching loop works in fixed steps of 7 pixels and random spacing, so changing the map size changes how many lines appear.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 58)
sections.title: Huts, trees and parcel numbers
sections.what: Draws each hut as a small dark rectangle, draws trees as circles with a dot in the middle, and draws palms as star shapes. It then writes numbers on every second visible field, starting at 401.
sections.why: Map symbols make the survey sheet easy to read at a glance.
sections.watch_out: The parcel numbers are made up from the list order, not from real records. Anyone reading the sheet could mistake them for official numbers.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 59)
sections.title: Shrine, office and satellite frame labels
sections.what: Draws a shrine symbol labelled Ghat and shrine, an office symbol labelled Anchal office, and a dashed rectangle labelled Satellite frame. The dashed box marks the area covered by the satellite picture.
sections.why: These landmarks orient the reader on the sheet.
sections.watch_out: The positions of the shrine, office and frame are fixed numbers on the sheet, so they will not move with the fields if the layout changes.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 60)
sections.title: Parcel boundaries and parcel label
sections.what: Draws three outlines of the same parcel: the historical record in dashed red, the survey in solid green, and the mapped geometry in dotted blue. It also writes the label DEMO-456 on a small box in the middle.
sections.why: Showing the three outlines together lets a reader see where the records disagree, which is the point of the tool.
sections.watch_out: The label is a demo value. Anyone using this map should not treat it as a real khesra number.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 61)
sections.title: Border, grid and title box
sections.what: Draws the outer border and inner frame, letter and number labels along the edges for a grid, and a title box in the top-left and a boundary note in the bottom-left. The title box says Example Mauza A and marks the sheet as synthetic.
sections.why: Grid references and a title make the sheet look like an official map, which helps users find places on it.
sections.watch_out: The title and note say synthetic and demo. Keep those words if this sheet is ever shown to a user, so it is not mistaken for a real record.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 62)
sections.title: Legend and scale bar
sections.what: Draws a legend explaining the three boundary lines, with their areas in acres. It also draws a scale bar marked 0 to 200 metres.
sections.why: A legend explains the line styles, and the scale bar tells the reader distances on the sheet.
sections.watch_out: The acre figures in the legend are typed in by hand, so they will not update if the parcel data changes.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 63)
sections.title: Compass arrow and grain setup
sections.what: Draws a north arrow with a red and a dark half and a letter N. It then creates a small noise image to use as paper grain.
sections.why: The north arrow tells the reader which way is up on the sheet. The grain makes the paper look real.
sections.watch_out: The grain image is created with the browser document object, so this code only works in a browser, not on the server.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: for
sections.title: Paper texture and cached image
sections.what: Lays the paper grain over the sheet and adds a darker edge around the sheet like an aged vignette. Then it saves the finished sheet as a JPEG image once and reuses it on later calls.
sections.why: Saving the image once avoids drawing the whole sheet again every time it is needed.
sections.watch_out: The image is saved as JPEG at 88 percent quality, so fine lines may look slightly blurred.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine: if
sections.title: Satellite thumbnails and map registration
sections.what: Draws two small satellite preview images from a fixed region of the painting, one with a faded look. Then it starts the function that registers each map display: it stores its size, watches for resizing, and prepares the pointer tracking.
sections.why: Each map display needs its own record so it is redrawn at the right size when the page changes.
sections.watch_out: Resizing uses a ResizeObserver when available, and falls back to a window resize listener otherwise. Both paths need to be cleaned up when a display is removed.

sections.name: getVillageSimulationEngine (part 66)
sections.title: Mouse tracking and public engine methods
sections.what: Tracks the pointer over the map and converts it into map coordinates, so nearby animals or walkers can react. It then returns the public methods other parts of the app use: register a display, set the pointer, get the survey image, draw thumbnails, check readiness, and wait for the painting to finish.
sections.why: This is the single doorway other parts of the app use to talk to the village picture.
sections.watch_out: The pointer listeners added to the window and document are never removed by the cleanup function, so removing a map display may leave listeners running.

summary: Builds and animates a painted village scene (fields, water, huts, trees, palms, cows, birds and drifting leaves) on hidden drawing areas, and returns a small controller that other code can use to show it on the page.
purpose: Gives the app a drawn, animated village map in a fixed and repeatable style, and provides a way to export the survey map as an image.
why: The header comment says the code was ported from a design HTML file. The code keeps the original random seeds and numbers so the look stays the same.
how: First, a repeatable random number generator is set up with a fixed seed. Second, the geography is defined: lake, ponds, islands, roads and a historic area. Third, fields, huts, trees, palms and cows are placed at random spots that respect water, roads and each other. Fourth, every painting step is queued in a list. Fifth, the queued steps run on a hidden canvas. Sixth, palm pictures are prepared separately. Seventh, moving elements such as birds, leaves, clouds and ripples are set up. Eighth, a per-frame update moves them and draws them onto the registered maps. Only the first 1894 lines are visible in this packet, so the per-frame loop and the exported functions are not reviewed here.
inputs: Map containers and canvas elements registered by callers, the pointer position, time values from the animation loop, and the browser reduced-motion setting.
outputs: A VillageSimulationEngine object with functions to register maps, set the pointer position, export the survey map as an image, draw satellite thumbnails, and report or wait for readiness.
risks: Heavy painting work runs when the engine starts, which can slow the page on load. The engine is a shared singleton, so all maps share its state. The palm drawing step swaps the drawing target without a safety net. Small edits to random call order or constants change the look of the whole village.
debug: If the scene is blank, check that the hidden painting canvas exists (it is only created when a document is present) and that the readiness check returns true. If birds or palms are missing, check the placement loops, which give up after a fixed number of tries. If the look changes unexpectedly, check whether random calls were added, removed or reordered. Look for canvas errors in the browser console. The later part of the file (line 1895 onward) is not reviewed here.
